blocks.content: 1. What Is Reliability?

A bank that is always online but occasionally transfers money to the wrong account is not actually serving its users. A hospital records system that responds instantly but sometimes pulls up the wrong patient's history is worse than useless, it is actively dangerous. Being up is not the same thing as being right, and this is exactly the domain reliability covers.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519051-934879328.png
blocks.alt: A system that never goes down but sometimes gives the wrong answer has not solved the problem it exists to solve

blocks.content: Reliability is the probability that a system performs its intended function correctly and consistently over a period of time, under defined operating conditions. Every word in that definition matters: correctly means the output is actually right, consistently means it stays right across many repeated uses, and under defined operating conditions means the guarantee only holds within the load and environment the system was actually built for.
2. The Core Distinction: Reliability vs Availability
blocks.text: 2. The Core Distinction: Reliability vs Availability

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519051-396026258.png
blocks.alt: Availability and reliability are independent axes, a system can score high on one and fail the other entirely

blocks.content: Availability, covered in its own topic, asks whether a system responds at all. Reliability asks a separate, arguably harder question: is that response actually correct? A system can be up 99.99% of the time while quietly returning wrong answers on 1% of requests, passing every uptime dashboard while genuinely failing its users.
Why Reliability Matters More Than Availability
blocks.text: Why Reliability Matters More Than Availability

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519819-668234364.png
blocks.alt: Users notice downtime and simply wait; wrong data is acted on before anyone realizes it was wrong

blocks.content: Users tolerate downtime far better than wrong answers. When a system is down, people know it, they wait, they retry later. When a system gives a wrong answer silently, people act on that wrong information immediately, transferring money, placing an order, or making a clinical decision, and by the time anyone notices the error, the damage is already done.
A 99.9% available system that is wrong 1% of the time is more dangerous than a 99% available system that is always correct.
3. Measuring Reliability: MTBF and MTTR
You cannot improve what you don't measure. Four metrics together give a complete operational picture: MTBF, MTTR, error rate, and data correctness rate.
Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519821-798467756.png
blocks.alt: MTBF answers exactly one question: how frequently does the system fail?

blocks.content: MTBF = Total Operating Time / Number of Failures. Example: a fleet runs for 8,400 hours and experiences 7 failures. MTBF = 8,400 / 7 = 1,200 hours, roughly one failure every 50 days for a single instance.

Scaled across a fleet of 300 identical services, expected failures per day = 300 x 24 hours / 1,200 hours = 6 failures per day across the whole fleet. MTBF turns an abstract sense of risk into concrete operational staffing, six failures a day means you need runbooks, on-call rotations, and automated recovery, not just hope that nothing breaks.
Mean Time To Recovery (MTTR)

MTBF tells you how often failures happen, MTTR tells you how fast you recover once one does. MTTR = Total Downtime / Number of Failures. Example: those same 7 failures caused 14 hours of total downtime, so MTTR = 14 / 7 = 2 hours per incident.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519821-639416190.png
blocks.alt: MTTR is the sum of four distinct phases, and each one can be independently shortened

blocks.content: MTTR is not simply repair time, it is the sum of detecting the failure, diagnosing its cause, actually repairing or failing over, and verifying the recovery held. Cutting MTTR, through better monitoring, automated failover, or clearer runbooks, frequently delivers more overall reliability improvement than trying to reduce the failure rate itself, since a fast, well-rehearsed recovery limits the blast radius of failures that are going to happen regardless.
4. Measuring Reliability: Error Rate and Data Correctness
blocks.text: 4. Measuring Reliability: Error Rate and Data Correctness

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519822-564959645.png
blocks.alt: A request can fail outright, or it can succeed while quietly returning the wrong answer, these are two different failure modes

blocks.content: Error Rate = Failed Requests / Total Requests x 100%, the fraction of requests that fail outright and visibly, an HTTP 500, a timeout, an exception. This is the easy half of the picture, because a failed request is, at least, obviously failed.

Data Correctness Rate = Correct Responses / Total Responses x 100%, the fraction of successful responses that actually contain correct data. This is the most overlooked metric, and often the most dangerous gap: monitoring can show 99.99% availability while 1% of users silently received wrong data and never knew it.

blocks.title: Correctness Must Be Measured Independently
blocks.content: Because a wrong-but-successful response looks identical to a right one on every standard uptime or error-rate dashboard, correctness requires its own dedicated measurement: data validation rules, checksums, shadow comparisons against a known-good system, and end-to-end tests against known expected outputs.
5. Why Systems Fail: Hardware
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271381221-417402672.png
blocks.alt: Physical components fail more at the very start and the very end of their life, and rarely in between

blocks.content: Physical components degrade following a bathtub curve: a higher failure rate early in life from manufacturing defects, which is exactly why burn-in testing exists; a long stretch of useful life with a low, stable failure rate, where MTBF estimates genuinely apply; and a rising wear-out phase at the end, since disks, capacitors, and batteries all carry known life limits.

At the scale of a large cluster, hardware failure stops being a rare event and becomes a constant, daily operational fact. Google has reported that across large fleets, disk failures, memory errors, and network packet corruption are simply ongoing background noise to be designed around, not exceptional incidents to be surprised by.
6. Why Systems Fail: Software Bugs
Unlike hardware failures, which are statistically random, software bugs are deterministic and systematic, every request that hits the same code path fails the exact same way.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271383148-229886798.png
blocks.alt: A crash is loud and gets fixed fast; a silent bug can run in production for months looking perfectly healthy

blocks.content: Bugs split by visibility: visible bugs crash loudly, throw an error, or return an obvious failure, and get noticed and fixed quickly. Silent bugs are far more dangerous, the system appears healthy by every availability and error-rate metric while quietly computing and returning the wrong result, exactly the correctness gap section 4 warns about.
7. Why Systems Fail: Configuration Errors
Configuration mistakes are responsible for a disproportionate share of major outages, a single wrong value can have system-wide impact far beyond what its size would suggest.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519823-301008402.png
blocks.alt: Three well-documented incidents, each triggered by a small configuration mistake with an outsized blast radius

blocks.content: {"headers":["Incident","What Happened","Impact"],"rows":[["Facebook, 2021","A BGP configuration command during routine maintenance withdrew Facebook's own IP routes from the global internet","Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger offline globally for roughly 6 hours"],["AWS S3, 2017","A debugging command meant to remove a small number of servers in a billing subsystem contained a typo that removed far more","S3 and every service depending on it degraded for hours across the US-EAST-1 region"],["GitLab, 2017","A database administrator running a replication fix accidentally deleted the production database instead of the staging one","Roughly 300GB of user data permanently lost"]]}
8. Why Systems Fail: Cascading Failures

This is the most architecturally interesting failure mode: one component slows down, and that slowness spreads until the entire system collapses, even though most of the components involved were never individually broken.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519823-576148904.png
blocks.alt: A single slow dependency, left unisolated, can turn into a full system outage through four predictable steps

blocks.content: ["The database becomes slow, due to a GC pause, a disk I/O issue, lock contention, or a hotspot, and starts responding much more slowly than normal","A downstream service waits longer for each database response, its threads stay busy longer, and its thread pool eventually fills up entirely, unable to process new requests","An upstream service depending on that downstream service starts seeing its own requests back up, its latency and resource usage climbing in turn","Clients time out and retry, adding even more load on top of an already struggling system, turning one slow dependency into a full, system-wide outage"]
items: The database becomes slow, due to a GC pause, a disk I/O issue, lock contention, or a hotspot, and starts responding much more slowly than normal
A downstream service waits longer for each database response, its threads stay busy longer, and its thread pool eventually fills up entirely, unable to process new requests
An upstream service depending on that downstream service starts seeing its own requests back up, its latency and resource usage climbing in turn
Clients time out and retry, adding even more load on top of an already struggling system, turning one slow dependency into a full, system-wide outage

blocks.content: The trigger was the database, the victims were every service downstream of it, none of which had anything individually wrong with them. Without isolation mechanisms like circuit breakers and timeouts, covered in sections 13 and 14, one slow dependency can cascade into a full outage entirely on its own.
9. Core Principle: Redundancy
No single point of failure: every component that matters has a standby, and if one instance fails, another absorbs the work without requiring a human to intervene.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271388307-25173020.png
blocks.alt: Redundancy comes in two forms, trading setup complexity against how much downtime a failure actually causes

blocks.content: {"headers":["","Active-Passive","Active-Active"],"rows":[["Setup","Simpler, one node stays idle most of the time","More complex, both nodes actively serve traffic"],["Failover Impact","Brief downtime during the switch","Little to no downtime"],["Cost","Idle standby node is pure cost overhead","Both nodes earn their keep, better resource utilization"],["Writes","Easy, only the primary ever handles writes","Write conflicts are possible since both nodes accept writes"]]}
10. Core Principle: Failover

Failover is the automatic process of switching to a backup when a primary fails. The word automatic is critical, a failover that requires a human to SSH in and run a command by hand is too slow and too risky under the pressure of a live incident.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519824-64360476.png
blocks.alt: An untested failover path is not actually a safety net, it is only a hope that one will work when needed

blocks.content: Failover must be tested regularly. A failover path that has never been exercised in production is not a genuine safety net, it is a false sense of security. Teams like Netflix run chaos engineering, deliberately and randomly killing production nodes, precisely to keep proving that failover actually works under real, live conditions rather than only in theory.
11. Techniques: Redundant Architecture and Data Replication
blocks.text: 11. Techniques: Redundant Architecture and Data Replication

blocks.content: Redundant architecture in practice: don't run a single server, run multiple. If one dies, the others keep serving traffic, with a load balancer in front watching their health and automatically routing around the failed one. The underlying rule is simple, any component that exists only once is a risk waiting to materialize.

Data replication follows the same logic for storage: never keep data in one place. Replicate it across multiple nodes or regions, so if the primary database crashes, a replica takes over and the data is still there.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271393649-234034225.png
blocks.alt: Synchronous and asynchronous replication trade write latency against how current the replica is guaranteed to be

blocks.content: ["Synchronous replication: waits for replicas to confirm before returning to the client, safer, since a confirmed write is genuinely durable on more than one node, but slower","Asynchronous replication: returns to the client immediately and replicates in the background, faster, but a replica can lag slightly behind and might not yet hold the very latest write"]
items: Synchronous replication: waits for replicas to confirm before returning to the client, safer, since a confirmed write is genuinely durable on more than one node, but slower
Asynchronous replication: returns to the client immediately and replicates in the background, faster, but a replica can lag slightly behind and might not yet hold the very latest write

blocks.content: 12. Techniques: Graceful Degradation

When parts of a system fail, don't let the whole thing go down with them. Shed non-critical features and keep the core working: a shopping site whose recommendation engine is down should still let customers complete checkout, rather than failing the entire page over one non-essential widget.

Every non-critical feature should have a defined fallback, not just an unhandled error. A recommendation section that cannot load should quietly disappear or show a generic fallback, never take the surrounding page down with it.
13. Techniques: Circuit Breakers

If a downstream service is failing, stop calling it. Every call that hangs ties up a thread, and enough hung threads bring your own service down too, even though nothing is actually wrong with your service's own code, exactly the cascading failure pattern from section 8.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271397125-325547462.png
blocks.alt: A circuit breaker moves through three states, closed, open, and half-open, to stop calling a failing dependency and safely test its recovery

blocks.content: A circuit breaker detects failures crossing a threshold, opens the circuit, and then fails requests instantly instead of waiting on a dependency that is unlikely to respond. After a cooldown period, it lets exactly one probe request through to check whether the dependency has recovered, closing the circuit again only if that probe succeeds. It protects your own service from being dragged down by someone else's problem.
14. Techniques: Idempotency, Timeouts, and Retries
Networks drop responses. Clients retry. Without idempotency, a retry means the operation runs twice, a payment gets charged twice, an order gets placed twice.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271399186-572699067.png
blocks.alt: An idempotency key lets a server recognize a retried request and return the original result instead of re-running the operation

blocks.content: The fix: attach a unique idempotency key to every request that has a side effect. The server stores the result the first time it processes that key, and if the exact same key arrives again, it returns the previously stored result without executing the operation a second time, making the retry safe by construction.

Every call to an external service also needs a timeout, without one a thread waits forever on a dependency that may never respond. A reasonable default is roughly 2x that service's normal response time. When a call does fail, retry with exponential backoff, waiting 1 second, then 2, then 4, rather than retrying instantly.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519825-48230357.png
blocks.alt: Exponential backoff spaces out retries; adding jitter keeps every client from retrying at the exact same instant

blocks.content: Adding a small amount of random jitter to each backoff interval keeps every client from retrying at the exact same moment, which would otherwise recreate the very overload the recovering service is trying to escape.
15. Techniques: Health Checks and Observability
A reliable system is one you can actually see into, blindness is not a reliability strategy, it just delays the moment you find out something is wrong.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519826-992112265.png
blocks.alt: Metrics, logs, and traces each answer a different question about the same failure

blocks.content: ["Metrics: numerical measurements collected over time, request rate, latency, CPU, memory. Tells you what is wrong, for example p99 latency suddenly jumping from 100ms to 2s","Logs: detailed event records of what happened at a specific moment, including error messages and stack traces. Tells you what happened and when, for example a database connection timeout logged at 10:05:32 AM","Traces: follow a single request as it travels through multiple services. Tells you where the problem actually is, for example a 3-second request where a trace shows 2.8 of those seconds were spent inside the payment service specifically"]
items: Metrics: numerical measurements collected over time, request rate, latency, CPU, memory. Tells you what is wrong, for example p99 latency suddenly jumping from 100ms to 2s

Logs: detailed event records of what happened at a specific moment, including error messages and stack traces. Tells you what happened and when, for example a database connection timeout logged at 10:05:32 AM

Traces: follow a single request as it travels through multiple services. Tells you where the problem actually is, for example a 3-second request where a trace shows 2.8 of those seconds were spent inside the payment service specifically

blocks.content: The example below implements the circuit breaker state machine from section 13 directly: a simulated dependency that fails for a stretch and later recovers, with the circuit breaker correctly opening after enough failures, rejecting calls instantly while open, and successfully closing again only once a probe request during the half-open state actually succeeds.
16. Reliability Checklist for Any Feature
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396519827-891738187.png
blocks.alt: Five questions worth asking before any new component ships

blocks.content: ["Redundancy: does every critical component have a backup instance, such that the failure of any single node does not affect users or bring down the system?","Dependency handling: do you understand how the system behaves when a dependency becomes slow or unavailable, and are timeouts and circuit breakers actually in place to stop that failure from spreading?","Data protection: is data protected through replication, idempotent writes, and a failover mechanism that has actually been tested, not just designed?","Observability: are metrics, logs, and traces all being collected, with alerts configured to catch problems quickly rather than relying on users to report them?","Recovery readiness: are there documented runbooks and, wherever possible, automated self-healing mechanisms, since the faster the recovery, the lower the impact on users?"]
items: Redundancy: does every critical component have a backup instance, such that the failure of any single node does not affect users or bring down the system?

Dependency handling: do you understand how the system behaves when a dependency becomes slow or unavailable, and are timeouts and circuit breakers actually in place to stop that failure from spreading?
Data protection: is data protected through replication, idempotent writes, and a failover mechanism that has actually been tested, not just designed?
Observability: are metrics, logs, and traces all being collected, with alerts configured to catch problems quickly rather than relying on users to report them?
Recovery readiness: are there documented runbooks and, wherever possible, automated self-healing mechanisms, since the faster the recovery, the lower the impact on users?

blocks.content: Worked Example

An online checkout service processes payments through a third-party payment gateway. To make it reliable: every payment request carries an idempotency key, so a network blip and client retry never double-charges a customer. A circuit breaker wraps every call to the payment gateway, so if the gateway itself starts failing, checkout fails fast with a clear "try again shortly" message instead of piling up hung threads waiting on a dead dependency.

The order database replicates synchronously to a standby in the same region, so a primary database failure triggers automatic failover with zero data loss, and asynchronously to a second region for disaster recovery, accepting a small replication lag there in exchange for surviving a full regional outage. Metrics track payment success rate and gateway latency continuously, and that failover path is deliberately tested through scheduled chaos-engineering drills, not assumed to work simply because it was designed correctly on paper.
Common Mistakes

["Treating availability metrics as proof of reliability, when a system can be up 99.99% of the time while silently returning wrong data on a meaningful fraction of requests","Building a failover mechanism and never actually testing it in a realistic, production-like failure scenario","Retrying failed requests without an idempotency key, turning a transient network blip into a duplicated payment or order","Adding retries without exponential backoff and jitter, which can turn a brief dependency hiccup into a self-inflicted thundering-herd overload","Measuring only error rate and never independently measuring data correctness, missing the exact gap where silent bugs do the most damage"]
items: Treating availability metrics as proof of reliability, when a system can be up 99.99% of the time while silently returning wrong data on a meaningful fraction of requests
Building a failover mechanism and never actually testing it in a realistic, production-like failure scenario
Retrying failed requests without an idempotency key, turning a transient network blip into a duplicated payment or order
Adding retries without exponential backoff and jitter, which can turn a brief dependency hiccup into a self-inflicted thundering-herd overload
Measuring only error rate and never independently measuring data correctness, missing the exact gap where silent bugs do the most damage

blocks.content: Practice

For a food delivery app's order-placement flow, walk through the reliability checklist from section 16 and identify, for each of the five questions, one concrete mechanism you would put in place, and one specific failure mode it directly protects against.

Then, using the cascading-failure walkthrough from section 8 as a template, describe how a sudden spike in restaurant-menu-image load times could cascade into a full outage of the order-placement flow, and name the specific technique from sections 12 through 14 that would stop it at each step.
Key Takeaways

Reliability is not the same axis as availability, a system can respond instantly and still be unreliable if what it returns is sometimes wrong, and users act on silent wrong answers far more readily than they tolerate visible downtime. MTBF and MTTR measure how often failures happen and how fast recovery is, while error rate and data correctness rate measure two genuinely different kinds of failure, one loud and one silent.

Systems fail through hardware wear, software bugs, configuration mistakes, and cascading failures, and the core defenses, redundancy, tested failover, circuit breakers, idempotency, timeouts with backoff and jitter, and real observability, exist specifically to contain each of those failure modes before they reach the user. The next topic, Single Point of Failure, looks specifically at identifying and eliminating the individual components whose failure alone can bring an entire system down.
